questions.prompt: Which security principle best applies to “Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)”?
options: Disable logs and tests so the security check cannot generate false positives.
Trust caller-controlled values and verify the control only on the successful happy path.
For cookie-authenticated state changes, apply the framework’s CSRF defenses and verify token/origin and cookie behavior; CORS is not an authentication or general CSRF substitute.
Rely on a hidden frontend control and skip backend verification because normal users cannot see the route.
questions.answer_key: For cookie-authenticated state changes, apply the framework’s CSRF defenses and verify token/origin and cookie behavior; CORS is not an authentication or general CSRF substitute.
questions.explanation: For cookie-authenticated state changes, apply the framework’s CSRF defenses and verify token/origin and cookie behavior; CORS is not an authentication or general CSRF substitute. The other choices rely on obscurity, remove useful verification, or trust input that should be treated as untrusted.

questions.prompt: You are reviewing “Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)” in an application you own or an explicitly authorized local lab. Which approach gives the strongest evidence that the intended control works?
options: Record real credentials and tokens in the report to make reproduction easier.
Write a focused test for the expected secure behavior and at least one relevant denied, malformed, expired, or failure case; record sanitized evidence.
Test only by looking at the page design and assume hidden controls are enforced.
Run broad tests against unrelated public systems to find a comparison point.
questions.answer_key: Write a focused test for the expected secure behavior and at least one relevant denied, malformed, expired, or failure case; record sanitized evidence.
questions.explanation: A useful security check has a defined scope, expected behavior, negative/failure coverage, and sanitized evidence. Never expand testing beyond permission or store secrets in evidence.

questions.prompt: If a check related to “Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)” fails unexpectedly, what is the best next step?
options: Reproduce with synthetic test data, compare expected and actual behavior, identify the root cause, apply a targeted fix, and retest neighboring paths.
Declare the entire application secure after a single successful request.
Change several unrelated settings at once and do not save the test conditions.
Suppress the finding without documenting why it is a false positive.
questions.answer_key: Reproduce with synthetic test data, compare expected and actual behavior, identify the root cause, apply a targeted fix, and retest neighboring paths.
questions.explanation: Reducing the case and retaining reproducible sanitized evidence supports root-cause analysis. A targeted regression test helps prevent the issue from returning.
